messages.content: Our bike shop keeps a movements ledger for parts - receipts in, issues out - but the items table also stores an on-hand number. How do I get the on-hand from the ledger itself, and should I trust it more than the stored number?
I'll build the ledger for one part, derive the balance from the movements alone, and then compare it with the stored counter:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE movements (movement_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, item TEXT NOT NULL, movement_date TEXT NOT NULL, movement_type TEXT NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE items (item TEXT PRIMARY KEY, stored_on_hand INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO items VALUES ('Inner tube 700x25', 160)
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN movement_type = 'receipt' THEN qty WHEN movement_type = 'issue' THEN -qty END) AS ledger_on_hand FROM movements WHERE item = 'Inner tube 700x25'
SELECT stored_on_hand FROM items WHERE item = 'Inner tube 700x25'

messages.content: The ledger derives 160 tubes on hand: receipts of 200 and 150 total 350, issues of 40, 65, 30 and 55 total 190, and 350 - 190 = 160. The stored counter on the items row says 160, so today the two agree. The point of deriving it anyway is which one you trust when they stop agreeing. The stored number is a claim; the ledger is the evidence. Every receipt and issue is a dated, individual fact, and the balance is just those facts added up with a sign convention - receipts positive, issues negative. If a tube is sold and the issue row is never written, the stored counter (if it is maintained by hand or by a separate process) can still be edited to look right while the ledger keeps the hole. Derive the balance from movements wherever you can, and treat any stored counter as a cache to be reconciled against the ledger, not as the truth itself.

The stored on-hand for our candle stock and my movements ledger are 7 units apart and I don't know when they split. Can you replay the ledger against the daily snapshots and find where they first disagree?
I'll build the week's movements and the stored daily snapshots, replay the ledger cumulatively, and compare day by day:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE movements (movement_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, movement_date TEXT NOT NULL, movement_type TEXT NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL, ref TEXT)
CREATE TABLE day_snapshots (day TEXT PRIMARY KEY, stored_balance INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT m.movement_date AS day, SUM(CASE WHEN m.movement_type = 'receipt' THEN m.qty ELSE -m.qty END) AS day_net FROM movements m GROUP BY m.movement_date ORDER BY m.movement_date

SELECT d.day, d.stored_balance, (SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN movement_type = 'receipt' THEN qty ELSE -qty END) FROM movements WHERE movement_date <= d.day) AS ledger_balance FROM day_snapshots d ORDER BY d.day
SELECT ref, COUNT(*) AS postings, SUM(qty) AS units FROM movements WHERE movement_type = 'issue' GROUP BY ref HAVING COUNT(*) > 1

messages.content: Replay the ledger day by day and compare it with the stored end-of-day balances. March 2 and 3 tie out exactly (108, then 99). The first divergence is 2026-03-04: the stored balance says 92 but the ledger sums to 85 - a gap of 7 units that never closes again (March 5: stored 81 vs ledger 74; March 6: stored 136 vs ledger 129). A constant gap that appears on one day and persists is the signature of a single bad posting on that day, not a counting drift. Grouping that day's issues by reference finds it: SO-107 was posted 2 times for 14 units total - the same 7-unit sale entered twice, once at the till and once from the paper ticket. The stored balance, which was decremented once, is the true one here; the ledger double-counts the issue. The fix is a reversing movement for the duplicate, not an edit to either number, so the correction itself stays in the audit trail. This is the general method: when a stored count and a derived count disagree, replay cumulatively and find the first day they part. Everything before that day is innocent; the defect lives in that day's postings.
My flour stock goes negative for two days in March and my manager thinks flour is vanishing. Can you run the balance through the movements and tell me what the negative actually means?
I'll build the flour movements and run the balance posting by posting:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE movements (movement_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, movement_date TEXT NOT NULL, movement_type TEXT NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL, note TEXT)

INSERT INTO movements VALUES (1, '2026-03-02', 'receipt', 80, 'flour delivery'), (2, '2026-03-03', 'issue', 100, 'bake for order B-220, picked Mar 3'), (3, '2026-03-05', 'receipt', 150, 'flour delivery booked Mar 5'), (4, '2026-03-06', 'issue', 60, 'bake for order B-224')

SELECT movement_date, movement_type, qty, SUM(CASE WHEN movement_type = 'receipt' THEN qty ELSE -qty END) OVER (ORDER BY movement_date, movement_id) AS running_balance FROM movements ORDER BY movement_id

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
movement_date | movement_type | qty | running_balance
2026-03-02 | receipt | 80 | 80
2026-03-03 | issue | 100 | -20
2026-03-05 | receipt | 150 | 130
2026-03-06 | issue | 60 | 70

arguments.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN movement_type = 'receipt' THEN qty ELSE -qty END) OVER (ORDER BY movement_date, movement_id) AS bal FROM movements) WHERE bal < 0

messages.content: The running balance tells the story: after the March 2 receipt of 80 kg the balance is 80; the March 3 issue of 100 kg drives it to -20; the March 5 receipt of 150 restores it to 130, and the March 6 issue leaves 70. Exactly 1 posting leaves the balance negative, and it is an artifact of dates, not of missing flour. The bakery really did bake order B-220 on March 3 using flour from a delivery that physically arrived that morning - but the goods receipt was only booked on March 5, when the paperwork caught up, while the issue was recorded on the day of the bake. Negative stock almost always means this: an issue carries the date the goods left, a receipt carries the date someone typed it in, and the two clocks disagree. Read negative balances as a dating problem first and a theft problem last. If you need the ledger to stay non-negative for reporting, book receipts with the delivery date from the delivery note, not the data-entry date - the movement_date should be when the stock moved, and a separate entered_at timestamp can carry when it was typed.

A customer just asked why their vanilla syrup order can't be fulfilled. I suspect the item is in our catalog but we've never actually stocked it. Can you check which catalog items have no stock movements at all, and whether any of them have open orders?
I'll build the cafe's catalog, its movements, and its open order lines, then anti-join the catalog against the ledger:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE items (item_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, item_name TEXT NOT NULL, listed_date TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO items VALUES (1, 'Espresso beans 1kg', '2025-11-03'), (2, 'Oat milk 1L', '2025-11-03'), (3, 'Vanilla syrup 750ml', '2026-01-19'), (4, 'Matcha powder 500g', '2026-02-02')
CREATE TABLE movements (movement_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, item_id INTEGER NOT NULL, movement_type TEXT NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO movements VALUES (1, 1, 'receipt', 40), (2, 1, 'issue', 33), (3, 2, 'receipt', 96), (4, 2, 'issue', 88), (5, 4, 'receipt', 10), (6, 4, 'issue', 2)
CREATE TABLE order_lines (order_id INTEGER NOT NULL, item_id INTEGER NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL, status TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO order_lines VALUES (501, 3, 6, 'open'), (502, 1, 5, 'open'), (503, 3, 2, 'open')
SELECT i.item_id, i.item_name FROM items i LEFT JOIN movements m ON m.item_id = i.item_id WHERE m.movement_id IS NULL

SELECT o.order_id, i.item_name, o.qty FROM order_lines o JOIN items i ON i.item_id = o.item_id WHERE o.status = 'open' AND i.item_id IN (SELECT item_id FROM items WHERE item_id NOT IN (SELECT DISTINCT item_id FROM movements))

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
order_id | item_name | qty
501 | Vanilla syrup 750ml | 6
503 | Vanilla syrup 750ml | 2

The LEFT JOIN finds the phantom: item 3, 'Vanilla syrup 750ml', sits in the catalog with zero movements of any kind - never received, never issued, never counted. Yet it is not idle: 2 open order lines promise it to customers - order 501 for 6 units and order 503 for 2 units, 8 units of a product the business has never physically held. This happens when a catalog item is created from a supplier listing or a menu plan before the first delivery ever lands, and ordering is allowed against the catalog alone. The stock query that protects you is exactly this anti-join: anything orderable must have at least a receipt in its history, and anything with open orders but no movements deserves a flag today, because those orders will fail at picking time and surprise a customer. Either the first delivery is genuinely coming (then the orders are pre-orders and should say so) or the item was listed by mistake and should be delisted until stock exists.
I want a running balance after every movement, per item, for our hardware store ledger - not just the final on-hand. Can you produce that view and point out anything worth noticing?
I'll build the two-item ledger and run a partitioned window sum over it:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE movements (movement_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, item TEXT NOT NULL, movement_date TEXT NOT NULL, movement_type TEXT NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL)

INSERT INTO movements VALUES (1, 'AA batteries 4pk', '2026-04-01', 'receipt', 120), (2, 'AA batteries 4pk', '2026-04-03', 'issue', 45), (3, 'AA batteries 4pk', '2026-04-06', 'issue', 50), (4, 'AA batteries 4pk', '2026-04-08', 'receipt', 80), (5, 'LED bulb E27', '2026-04-02', 'receipt', 60), (6, 'LED bulb E27', '2026-04-05', 'issue', 18), (7, 'LED bulb E27', '2026-04-07', 'issue', 18), (8, 'LED bulb E27', '2026-04-09', 'issue', 24)

SELECT item, movement_date, movement_type, qty, SUM(CASE WHEN movement_type = 'receipt' THEN qty ELSE -qty END) OVER (PARTITION BY item ORDER BY movement_date, movement_id) AS running_balance FROM movements ORDER BY item, movement_id

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
item | movement_date | movement_type | qty | running_balance
AA batteries 4pk | 2026-04-01 | receipt | 120 | 120
AA batteries 4pk | 2026-04-03 | issue | 45 | 75
AA batteries 4pk | 2026-04-06 | issue | 50 | 25
AA batteries 4pk | 2026-04-08 | receipt | 80 | 105
LED bulb E27 | 2026-04-02 | receipt | 60 | 60
LED bulb E27 | 2026-04-05 | issue | 18 | 42
LED bulb E27 | 2026-04-07 | issue | 18 | 24
LED bulb E27 | 2026-04-09 | issue | 24 | 0

The window function keeps a separate running balance per item. Batteries end at 105 after a mid-month receipt refilled them. The bulbs tell a quieter story: 60 received, then issues of 18, 18 and 24 walk the balance 60 -> 42 -> 24 -> 0. The last issue exactly empties the shelf - the balance lands on zero, not below it, so nothing in the ledger is wrong; the item is simply out, and because issues stop appearing after April 9 the ledger alone cannot tell you whether demand stopped or the empty shelf stopped it. Partitioned running balances are the workhorse view of a movements ledger: one pass gives you the balance after every posting for every item, which is what you need for spotting near-stockouts (balances that touched single digits), exact-empty landings like this one, and any posting that pushed a balance below zero. Order by date and then by movement_id inside the partition - when two postings share a date, the id is the only honest tiebreak for the order they were booked.

An insurer is asking what our stock of paint was at the end of February, but our system only shows today's count. The movements ledger goes back to January. Can you reconstruct the February 28 balance from it?
I'll build the paint ledger and sum it with a date ceiling for the February position, then the full sum for today:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE movements (movement_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, movement_date TEXT NOT NULL, movement_type TEXT NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN movement_type = 'receipt' THEN qty ELSE -qty END) AS balance FROM movements WHERE movement_date <= '2026-02-28'
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN movement_type = 'receipt' THEN qty ELSE -qty END) AS balance FROM movements
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN movement_type = 'receipt' THEN qty ELSE -qty END) AS march_net FROM movements WHERE movement_date BETWEEN '2026-03-01' AND '2026-03-31'

messages.content: Because the balance is derived, any past date is just a filter. At February 28 the ledger sums to 175 units (300 in, 125 out). March's net movement is 110 (200 in, 90 out), and the all-time sum to today is 245. The two numbers are consistent by construction: 175 + 110 = 285, which is the balance at March 31, and April's issue of 40 brings it to 245. This is the audit superpower of a movements ledger over a stored counter: a stored counter can only tell you now, and last month's number is gone the moment it is overwritten. The ledger can rebuild the stock position for any date an auditor, an insurer, or a tax question asks about - provided movements are never edited or deleted, only reversed. One discipline makes or breaks it: backdated corrections must be posted as new movements dated today with a note, not by rewriting an old row's date, or every historical reconstruction after that date silently changes.

Our warehouse ledger has more movement types than just receipts and issues - transfers both ways, adjustments, damage write-offs. Can you net them all out by type and give me the true balance with the sign conventions made explicit?
I'll build a quarter of mixed movements for one SKU and net them by type:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE movements (movement_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, movement_type TEXT NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL)

INSERT INTO movements VALUES (1, 'receipt', 500), (2, 'issue', 210), (3, 'issue', 130), (4, 'transfer_in', 60), (5, 'transfer_out', 45), (6, 'adjustment', -8), (7, 'damage_writeoff', 12), (8, 'receipt', 200), (9, 'issue', 75)
SELECT movement_type, COUNT(*) AS postings, SUM(qty) AS units FROM movements GROUP BY movement_type ORDER BY movement_type

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
movement_type | postings | units
adjustment | 1 | -8
damage_writeoff | 1 | 12
issue | 3 | 415
receipt | 2 | 700
transfer_in | 1 | 60
transfer_out | 1 | 45

arguments.sql: SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN movement_type IN ('receipt', 'transfer_in') THEN qty WHEN movement_type = 'adjustment' THEN qty ELSE -qty END) AS net_balance FROM movements

messages.content: Netting by type shows the quarter's whole story in one table. Inflows: receipts 700 and transfers in 60. Outflows: issues 415, transfers out 45, damage write-offs 12. The adjustment row is already signed (-8), so the net balance is 700 + 60 - 415 - 45 - 12 - 8 = 280. Two design points matter here. First, sign conventions must be decided per movement type and written down: receipts and transfers-in add, issues and transfers-out subtract, and adjustments are the one type where the sign lives in the quantity itself, because an adjustment can correct in either direction. Second, damage write-offs deserve their own type rather than being folded into issues - issues are demand, write-offs are loss, and any report that mixes them will overstate sales and hide shrinkage. The GROUP BY over movement_type is the cheapest integrity view there is: if a type appears that is not in your convention list, the netting formula is silently wrong for it.

I think some shipments went out without the stock issue ever being posted, which would leave our on-hand too high. Can you cross-check shipments against ledger issues and find any that never hit stock?
I'll build the pet-supply shipments and the ledger, then look for shipments with no matching issue:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE shipments (shipment_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, ship_date TEXT NOT NULL, item TEXT NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE movements (movement_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, movement_date TEXT NOT NULL, movement_type TEXT NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL, shipment_ref INTEGER)
SELECT s.shipment_id, s.ship_date, s.qty FROM shipments s LEFT JOIN movements m ON m.shipment_ref = s.shipment_id AND m.movement_type = 'issue' WHERE m.movement_id IS NULL
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN movement_type = 'receipt' THEN qty ELSE -qty END) FROM movements

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
SUM(CASE WHEN movement_type = 'receipt' THEN qty ELSE -qty END)
145

The anti-join finds it: shipment 3 on 2026-05-06 sent 30 leashes out the door with no matching issue in the ledger. The ledger therefore says 145 on hand, but the shelf truth is 200 received minus 85 shipped = 115. The stock is overstated by exactly the missing issue's 30 units. This is the most common ledger hole in small operations: the shipment is real (a carrier label exists, the customer got the goods), but the stock issue was a separate manual step that got skipped on a busy day. The defensive query is the one just run - every shipment should join to exactly one issue, and the exceptions list should be empty every morning. When you find one, post the issue now, dated with the shipment date and referencing the shipment, rather than quietly editing the stored count: the ledger then shows both the mistake and its repair, and the next person reconciling May does not have to guess which number moved.

Our cola stock shows a crazy negative-ish balance even though the shelf looks fine. We buy by the case of 12 and sell by the can, and both go into the same movements table. Can you show me what the balance looks like summed raw versus converted to one unit?
I'll build the mixed-unit ledger and sum it both ways:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE movements (movement_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, movement_date TEXT NOT NULL, movement_type TEXT NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL, uom TEXT NOT NULL)
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN movement_type = 'receipt' THEN qty ELSE -qty END) AS raw_balance FROM movements
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN movement_type = 'receipt' THEN qty * 12 ELSE -qty END) AS unit_balance FROM movements

messages.content: Summed raw, the ledger says -98 - receipts of 10 and 5 against issues of 34, 51 and 28. That number is meaningless, because it adds cases and units as if they were the same thing: the warehouse books cola in by the case of 12 and the shop sells it by the can. Convert receipts to base units in the query and the same ledger reads 67 cans: (10 + 5) x 12 = 180 in, 113 out. Nothing about the data changed; the unit of measure was simply part of the quantity all along, and ignoring it manufactured a phantom shortage of 165 units. Unit-of-measure mismatches are a classic source of 'impossible' stock: receipts in cases, issues in units, counts in pallets. The durable fixes are to store every movement in one base unit at posting time (converting at the door, with the original quantity and UOM kept in note fields), or to carry a units_per_pack column and convert in every query - the first is safer, because a conversion that lives in queries will be forgotten by the one query that matters. If your ledger already mixes units, a uom column plus a CASE like this one is the honest bridge until the data is normalized.

We only started keeping a movements ledger on March 1, and summing it gives a balance that's way below what's on the shelf, with a negative dip in the first week. What is the ledger missing and how do I anchor it properly?
I'll build the March-only ledger, sum it as-is, then post the opening count as its own movement type and sum again:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE movements (movement_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, movement_date TEXT NOT NULL, movement_type TEXT NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN movement_type = 'receipt' THEN qty ELSE -qty END) FROM movements

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
SUM(CASE WHEN movement_type = 'receipt' THEN qty ELSE -qty END)
67

arguments.sql: INSERT INTO movements VALUES (0, '2026-03-01', 'opening_balance', 300)
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN movement_type IN ('receipt', 'opening_balance') THEN qty ELSE -qty END) FROM movements

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
SUM(CASE WHEN movement_type IN ('receipt', 'opening_balance') THEN qty ELSE -qty END)
367

March's movements alone net to 67 (210 in, 143 out) - and for the first week the running balance is negative, which looks alarming until you remember the ledger only started on March 1. The shop did not open in March; the bookkeeping did. Posting the March 1 physical count as an explicit opening_balance movement of 300 makes the ledger self-contained: the full sum is now 367, and every balance from March 1 onward is real. Every movements ledger needs this anchor. Without an opening row, derived balances are only correct relative to an unknown starting point, and anyone summing the table gets a number that is wrong by exactly the opening stock - here, wrong by 300 against a true {with_open[0][0]}. The opening balance should come from an actual count taken on the day the ledger starts, be posted as its own movement type (never disguised as a receipt, which would corrupt purchasing history), and be the one row in the table that is allowed to be an estimate - it is a counted fact about the shelf, not a transaction.
How do I set a reorder point for our packing tape from actual usage? I have the last month of issues and the supplier says lead time is 5 days.
I'll build the month's issue history, derive average daily usage, and apply the reorder-point formula:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE issues (issue_date TEXT NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT SUM(qty) AS units_30d, COUNT(DISTINCT issue_date) AS issue_days, MAX(qty) AS biggest_day FROM issues

messages.content: The tape leaves the shelf steadily: 240 units issued over the 30 days of April, which is 240 / 30 = 8.0 units a day. (Issues happened on 11 distinct days; daily usage for reorder math is total demand over calendar days, not over days that happened to have a sale, or quiet days would inflate the rate.) The supplier takes 5 days from order to delivery, so the stock must cover 5 days of demand while the order travels: reorder point = 8.0 x 5 = 40 units. When the balance touches 40, order - in the average world the last unit leaves the shelf the hour the delivery arrives. Two honest caveats belong with the number. This ROP assumes demand is smooth, and real demand is lumpy - the biggest single day here took 26 - which is what safety stock exists for. And the lead time is the supplier's quoted 5 days; the lead time you should plan on is the one measured from your own receipts, which is often longer. The formula is simple on purpose: daily usage x lead days. Everything sophisticated in reorder logic is an argument about what numbers to feed those two slots.
Average-based reorder points keep failing us on busy days. Is there a simple safety stock method I can compute from our daily issue history for exam gloves? Lead time is 5 days.
I'll build eleven days of issues, pull the average and the peak, and apply the simple max-minus-average safety stock rule:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE daily_issues (day TEXT NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT ROUND(AVG(qty), 2) AS avg_daily, MAX(qty) AS max_daily, SUM(qty) AS total FROM daily_issues

messages.content: Eleven days of glove issues total 88 units: an average of 8.0 a day, but a peak day of 14. The plain reorder point (average x lead time) is 8 x 5 = 40, and it fails precisely on the days that look like the 14-unit day - if a surge starts the morning you reorder, 40 units is gone in three days and the delivery is still two days out. The simple safety-stock method - and it is deliberately simple - insures the gap between average and peak: (14 - 8) x 5 = 30 extra units, giving a working reorder point of 70. The method's honesty is in what it ignores: it treats the single worst observed day as the shape of every day in the lead window, which over-insures if the peak was a one-off and under-insures if demand is growing. More formal methods use the standard deviation of daily demand and a service-level target; they are better statistics and worse explanations. For a small operation this max-minus-average rule has the right virtues: it is computed from your own worst day, it is one line of arithmetic anyone can re-check, and its cost is visible - 30 units of gloves sitting still is the price of not running out, stated in units instead of hidden in a formula.

Our shampoo reorder point keeps getting lower every cycle and the stockouts keep getting longer, which feels backwards. June's daily issues and end-of-day balances are in a table. Can you show me what the stockout itself is doing to my usage calculation?
I'll build June day by day, count the zero-balance days, and compute usage both ways - over the calendar and over stocked days only:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE daily (day TEXT NOT NULL, issued INTEGER NOT NULL, end_balance INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT SUM(issued) AS total_issued, SUM(CASE WHEN end_balance = 0 AND issued = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS zero_days FROM daily

messages.content: June's shampoo history is a trap for the average. The shelf emptied during June 8 and then sat at zero for 22 of the month's 30 days, so issues total only 100 - not because demand stopped, but because an empty shelf cannot issue anything. Divide by the calendar and you get 3.3333333333 units a day, which sets a 6-day-lead reorder point of about 20. But demand only had 8 stocked days to express itself in: 100 / 8 = 12.5 units a day, and the honest reorder point is 12.5 x 6 = 75. The naive figure under-orders by a factor of almost four and guarantees the stockout repeats - each empty period poisons the next average, which lowers the next reorder point, which lengthens the next empty period. Statisticians call the zero days censored demand: the instrument (issues) measures min(demand, stock), not demand. The practical corrections are to compute usage over stocked days only, as here, or to add back recorded unfilled orders where you have them. What you must not do is feed raw issues from a window containing a stockout into a reorder formula and call the result demand.

Someone told me to use EOQ for our coffee bean orders. I have a year of monthly issues, an ordering cost of about $45 per order, and holding cost around $1.20 per unit per year. Can you compute it - and tell me what the formula is quietly assuming?
I'll total the year's issues for annual demand, then run the EOQ formula once, with the assumptions laid out after:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE issues (issue_date TEXT NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT SUM(qty) AS annual_units FROM issues

messages.content: A year of monthly issues totals 2400 units of coffee beans - that is the D in the formula. With an ordering cost S of 4500 cents ($45 of staff time, delivery fees and paperwork per order, however it is placed) and a holding cost H of 120 cents per unit per year (the shelf space, the capital, the spoilage risk on one bag-slot for a year), EOQ = sqrt(2 x 2400 x 4500 / 120) = sqrt(180000) = about 424 bags per order, roughly five or six orders a year. Now the assumptions, which are the actual content of the model: demand is constant and known (yours ranges 175-230 a month, so, approximately), ordering cost is the same however much you order, holding cost is linear in units and time, lead time is fixed, and there are no quantity discounts, no spoilage cliff, and no storage cap. EOQ earns its keep as a scale check, not an oracle: it tells you whether you are ordering in the right ballpark - if you currently order 50 bags at a time, you are paying ordering costs far more often than the tradeoff justifies; if you order 2,000, you are warehousing beans. When its assumptions fail badly - lumpy project demand, a supplier discount at 500 - the assumption that fails should set the order size instead, and the formula's job was to make you say which one.

Our supplier quotes 5-day lead time but deliveries feel all over the place. I have order and receipt dates for the last eight purchase orders. What lead time should I actually plan reorder points on, at 9 units a day?
I'll compute the actual lead time of every order from its dates and compare promise, average and worst case:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE purchase_orders (po_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, order_date TEXT NOT NULL, promised_days INTEGER NOT NULL, received_date TEXT)
SELECT po_id, CAST(julianday(received_date) - julianday(order_date) AS INTEGER) AS actual_lead_days, promised_days FROM purchase_orders ORDER BY actual_lead_days DESC
SELECT ROUND(AVG(julianday(received_date) - julianday(order_date)), 1) AS avg_lead, MAX(CAST(julianday(received_date) - julianday(order_date) AS INTEGER)) AS max_lead FROM purchase_orders

messages.content: The supplier promises 5 days on every order. The receipts tell a different story: actual lead times run 6 to 13 days, averaging 7.8. Two orders took 10 and 13 days - the 13-day one is PO 5 in April, when a 5-day promise met reality. Plan a reorder point on the promised 5 days at 9 units a day and you hold 45 units of cover; the April delivery would have needed 9 x 13 = 117. Even the average (7.8 days) only covers the typical order, and stockouts are by definition caused by the atypical ones. Planning on the longest observed lead time - 9 x 13 = 117 units of lead-time demand - is the conservative small-shop rule: it insures against the worst delivery you have actually experienced. Its cost is real (more stock sitting still) and so is its limit: eight orders is a small sample, and the true worst case is worse than the worst you have seen. The middle path most operations land on is average lead time for the base reorder point plus safety stock sized from lead-time variability - but whichever you choose, measure lead time from your own PO and receipt dates, never from the quote. The quote is a marketing document; the receipts are data.
I want a morning list of everything that needs reordering - derived from the movements ledger, not from a stored count, with how far below the point each item is. Can you build that?
I'll set up the office-supply items with their reorder points, derive balances from the ledger, and filter to the ones at or below the line:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE items (item TEXT PRIMARY KEY, reorder_point INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO items VALUES ('Copy paper A4', 60), ('Toner cartridge TN-240', 8), ('Sticky notes 76mm', 40), ('Ballpoint pens blue', 100), ('Archive boxes', 25)
CREATE TABLE movements (movement_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, item TEXT NOT NULL, movement_type TEXT NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL)

Our candles sell steadily all year and then explode in November and December, and the annual-average reorder point failed us last Christmas. Can you quantify how far off it is for a 7-day lead time?

The annual-average point under-covers the season by roughly 46 units: in the first week of the rush, the shelf empties while a correctly-sized order is still in transit, and it happens at the exact moment the item earns its year. Seasonal items need seasonal parameters: compute usage over the comparable season last year, not over the trailing twelve months, and let the reorder point step up before the season and back down after it. The failure mode to avoid is the opposite one - leaving December's point in place all year and warehousing candles in July. A simple calendar of parameter sets (normal / peak) driven by last year's monthly shape beats a single annual average at both ends.

messages.content: Audit the policy against the ledger: with a reorder point of 40, the running balance first touches the line on 2026-04-09 (balance 38). The purchase order was not placed until 2026-04-13 - 4 days after the crossing. By then the balance had already fallen through zero on 2026-04-15, and the shelf sat empty until the receipt on April 20. The reorder point did not fail; it fired on time and nobody acted for 4 days. Some of lot L-2215's tubs were almost certainly counted as L-2214 - the lots sit side by side, their labels differ by one digit, and L-2215's own count (255 against 260 received, with issues since) is consistent with a few of its tubs wearing the wrong lot number in the count. This is why lot counts reconcile against receipts per lot, not in aggregate: in aggregate the yogurt count looks plausible, and the impossibility only appears when the lot is forced to balance against its own receiving history. The fix is a recount of the two lots side by side, reading labels rather than counting tubs and splitting the difference - and a process note: adjacent lots with near-identical codes are a known counting hazard, so the count sheet should print lot codes in full with the expiry date beside them as a second check.

I'll build the freeze snapshot and the during-window movements, then compute raw and reconciled variances side by side:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE count_snapshot (item TEXT PRIMARY KEY, book_at_freeze INTEGER NOT NULL, counted_qty INTEGER NOT NULL, freeze_time TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO count_snapshot VALUES ('Olive oil 750ml', 120, 118, '2026-07-11 09:00'), ('Balsamic vinegar', 64, 64, '2026-07-11 09:00'), ('Sea salt flakes', 45, 41, '2026-07-11 09:00')
CREATE TABLE movements (movement_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, item TEXT NOT NULL, posted_at TEXT NOT NULL, movement_type TEXT NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL)

INSERT INTO movements VALUES (1, 'Olive oil 750ml', '2026-07-11 08:15', 'issue', 5), (2, 'Olive oil 750ml', '2026-07-11 09:40', 'issue', 7), (3, 'Olive oil 750ml', '2026-07-11 10:05', 'receipt', 24), (4, 'Sea salt flakes', '2026-07-11 09:20', 'issue', 4), (5, 'Balsamic vinegar', '2026-07-11 11:30', 'issue', 3)

SELECT c.item, c.book_at_freeze, c.counted_qty, c.counted_qty - c.book_at_freeze AS raw_variance, COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN m.movement_type = 'receipt' THEN m.qty ELSE -m.qty END), 0) AS during_count_net, c.counted_qty - (c.book_at_freeze + COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN m.movement_type = 'receipt' THEN m.qty ELSE -m.qty END), 0)) AS true_variance FROM count_snapshot c LEFT JOIN movements m ON m.item = c.item AND m.posted_at > c.freeze_time GROUP BY c.item, c.book_at_freeze, c.counted_qty ORDER BY c.item

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
item | book_at_freeze | counted_qty | raw_variance | during_count_net | true_variance
Balsamic vinegar | 64 | 64 | 0 | -3 | 3
Olive oil 750ml | 120 | 118 | -2 | 17 | -19
Sea salt flakes | 45 | 41 | -4 | -4 | 0

The count was frozen at 09:00 but the shop kept trading, and three movements posted during the count window. Raw variances say olive oil is short 2 and sea salt is short 4. Reconcile against the during-window movements and the picture splits. Olive oil: book at freeze 120, then an issue of 7 and a receipt of 24 posted mid-count (net 17), so the shelf the counters actually faced should have held 137 - they found 118, a true variance of -19. The mid-count receipt makes the shortage worse, not better: 19 units are unexplained even after the trading is accounted for, and that one is real and needs investigation. Sea salt is the opposite: its raw -4 is exactly the 4-unit issue posted at 09:20 while the counters were in the next aisle - true variance 0, no loss at all, just a count compared against a stale book. A count freeze that the business cannot honor has to be reconciled, not believed: variance = counted - (book at freeze + net movements during the window). Any count process that skips the second term manufactures shrinkage on busy count days and teaches staff to distrust every number the count produces.

We run a store and a warehouse and transfers between them keep muddying the stock picture. Can you give me per-location balances and the company total for one shoe model, and check the transfers for completeness?
I'll build the two-location ledger, derive balances per location and in total, and look for transfer legs that never landed:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE movements (movement_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, item TEXT NOT NULL, location TEXT NOT NULL, movement_type TEXT NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL)

INSERT INTO movements VALUES (1, 'Trail shoes M10', 'Store', 'receipt', 40), (2, 'Trail shoes M10', 'Store', 'issue', 17), (3, 'Trail shoes M10', 'Store', 'transfer_out', 12), (4, 'Trail shoes M10', 'Warehouse', 'receipt', 85), (5, 'Trail shoes M10', 'Warehouse', 'issue', 30), (6, 'Trail shoes M10', 'Warehouse', 'transfer_out', 12)
SELECT location, SUM(CASE WHEN movement_type = 'receipt' THEN qty ELSE -qty END) AS balance FROM movements GROUP BY location ORDER BY location
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN movement_type = 'receipt' THEN qty ELSE -qty END) AS total FROM movements

messages.content: Per location, the shoes stand at 43 in the Warehouse and 11 in the Store - the locations sum to 54. Now audit the transfer: 12 pairs left the store (transfer_out) and 12 left the warehouse in a separate transfer_out - but no transfer_in exists anywhere in the ledger. Two transfers out and none in means 24 pairs are in a truck, in a corridor, or in a data hole. The company received 125 pairs and issued 47, so 78 pairs exist somewhere - yet the two location balances account for only 54. If the store's 12 were physically received at the warehouse and simply never booked in, the warehouse truly holds 43 + 12 = 55 and the store's 11 is real, but the ledger cannot tell you that; it can only tell you the ins are missing. In-transit stock is where multi-location ledgers go to die: a transfer is two movements with a time gap, and any report run inside the gap - or forever, if the second leg is forgotten - misstates both ends. The disciplines that keep it honest: transfers carry a shared transfer reference so the anti-join 'out-legs with no in-leg' can be run daily (it should return nothing older than the normal transit time), and in-transit is reported as its own location in stock reports, so the missing 24 pairs would have appeared as a visible 'In transit: 24' line instead of vanishing from both shelves.
We stock the same yogurt in four lots with different expiry dates and an order for 150 tubs just came in. Show me the FEFO pick - which lots it should draw from and how much from each.
I'll build the lot table and run the lots in expiry order with a running total:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE lots (lot TEXT PRIMARY KEY, item TEXT NOT NULL, expiry_date TEXT NOT NULL, qty_on_hand INTEGER NOT NULL)

INSERT INTO lots VALUES ('Y-0312', 'Natural yogurt 1kg', '2026-08-14', 40), ('Y-0326', 'Natural yogurt 1kg', '2026-08-21', 65), ('Y-0402', 'Natural yogurt 1kg', '2026-08-28', 80), ('Y-0416', 'Natural yogurt 1kg', '2026-09-04', 55)

SELECT lot, expiry_date, qty_on_hand, SUM(qty_on_hand) OVER (ORDER BY expiry_date) - qty_on_hand AS cum_before, SUM(qty_on_hand) OVER (ORDER BY expiry_date) AS cum_through FROM lots ORDER BY expiry_date

messages.content: FEFO - first expiry, first out - is just the lots sorted by expiry date with a running total, and the pick for today's order of 150 tubs walks straight down it: lot Y-0312 (expires 2026-08-14): 40 on hand, cumulative through this lot 40; lot Y-0326 (expires 2026-08-21): 65 on hand, cumulative through this lot 105; lot Y-0402 (expires 2026-08-28): 80 on hand, cumulative through this lot 185; lot Y-0416 (expires 2026-09-04): 55 on hand, cumulative through this lot 240. The order takes all 40 of the August 14 lot and all 65 of the August 21 lot (105), then 150 - 105 = 45 from the August 28 lot, leaving 35 of that lot and the September lot untouched. Why the order matters more than the arithmetic: picking newest-first feels identical at the till and completely different in the waste bin - the August 14 lot would sit while fresher stock ships, expire in place, and convert silently from inventory to write-off. FEFO must live in the pick list the picker sees, sorted and allocated by the system, because no human scanning a cold room will reliably reconstruct expiry order under time pressure. One refinement separates good implementations: the allocation should also respect a minimum remaining shelf life the customer or channel requires - a lot can be unexpired and still unshippable to a customer who needs 10 days of life on receipt.

A picker just got sent to a milk lot that expired three days ago. Our FEFO pick query just takes the earliest expiry with stock. Can you show me what it picks versus what it should pick today, August 12?
I'll build the milk lots and run the pick query as-is, then with the filters it is missing:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE lots (lot TEXT PRIMARY KEY, item TEXT NOT NULL, expiry_date TEXT NOT NULL, qty_on_hand INTEGER NOT NULL, status TEXT NOT NULL)

INSERT INTO lots VALUES ('M-118', 'Whole milk 2L', '2026-08-09', 22, 'active'), ('M-121', 'Whole milk 2L', '2026-08-16', 48, 'active'), ('M-124', 'Whole milk 2L', '2026-08-23', 60, 'active'), ('M-109', 'Whole milk 2L', '2026-08-02', 0, 'active')
SELECT lot, expiry_date, qty_on_hand FROM lots WHERE qty_on_hand > 0 ORDER BY expiry_date LIMIT 1
SELECT lot, expiry_date, qty_on_hand FROM lots WHERE qty_on_hand > 0 AND expiry_date >= '2026-08-12' AND status = 'active' ORDER BY expiry_date LIMIT 1

messages.content: Today is August 12. The naive pick query - earliest expiry with stock, nothing else - sends the picker to lot M-118, which expired on 2026-08-09: 22 bottles of out-of-date milk, still flagged active, still holding a quantity, and first in line precisely because FEFO sorts by expiry and expired stock has the earliest date of all. The corrected query adds the two filters that make FEFO safe - expiry_date >= today and status active - and picks lot M-121 (expires 2026-08-16, 48 on hand). The deeper problem is that lot M-118 exists in this state at all: expiry should be an event, not a discovery. A daily job (or a daily query reviewed by a human) listing lots whose expiry has passed with qty > 0 turns the expired lot into a same-day write-off and a quarantine move, and the pick query's date filter becomes a second line of defense instead of the only one. Defense in depth is the pattern: prevent expired stock from being pickable in the query, and separately hunt it in the data, because either check alone will eventually be the one that was skipped.

transfer_ref | out_qty | in_qty | in_transit
TR-77 | 30 | 30 | 0

A transfer has a lifecycle, and the ledger shows all three states. TR-77: 30 out of North on September 3, 30 into South on September 5 - complete, in-transit 0, having spent two days as stock that existed but was on neither shelf. TR-79 went out and in the same day. TR-78 is still open: 18 units out of North on September 4 and no in-leg - 18 units in transit, or lost, or sitting in South's goods-in cage unbooked; the ledger cannot distinguish those, which is exactly why open transfers past their expected transit time get a daily exception report. The accounting identity to hold onto: out minus in, per transfer reference, is the in-transit balance, and the sum over all references is the company's in-transit stock. Any stock report that only sums shelf locations will understate total stock by that amount, and any availability promise made from the sending store the moment the out-leg posts is honest, while the receiving store must not promise the goods until the in-leg posts. Model the gap explicitly - a location called IN_TRANSIT that transfers move into and out of - and the two-leg transfer becomes two ordinary movements that every existing report already understands.

Can you check our bins against their capacities? If any bin claims to hold more than it physically can, I want to know - that has to be a data error.
I'll total the stock per bin against the bin master capacities:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE bins (bin TEXT PRIMARY KEY, capacity INTEGER NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE bin_stock (bin TEXT NOT NULL, item TEXT NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL)

INSERT INTO bin_stock VALUES ('B-01', 'Bolts M8', 72), ('B-01', 'Washers M8', 20), ('B-02', 'Bolts M10', 98), ('B-03', 'Screws 4x40', 45), ('B-03', 'Wall plugs 6mm', 30), ('B-04', 'Hinges 100mm', 61), ('B-05', 'Cable 100m drums', 150)

Either a receipt was booked into the wrong bin (the neighboring bin's count will be short by the same amount), the capacity on the bin master is stale after a re-racking, or two items' quantities were merged under one bin during a rushed putaway. The over-capacity query is worth running weekly precisely because it cannot produce false alarms of the 'maybe it's fine' kind: every row it returns is definitely wrong somewhere. Treat capacity as a soft physical model, though - it is in units here, and real bins constrain volume and weight, so a bin of foam can be 'full' at 30 units while a bin of bolts takes 500. The check earns its keep as an impossibility detector at the extremes, not as a precise space planner; set capacities in the unit that actually binds for that bin's typical contents.

An order for 500 jars of jam needs to be picked FEFO across three lots of 200, 200 and 150. Can you compute the exact per-lot pick quantities?
I'll order the lots by expiry with a cumulative-before column and cap each lot's take at the remaining need:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE lots (lot TEXT PRIMARY KEY, expiry_date TEXT NOT NULL, qty_on_hand INTEGER NOT NULL)

SELECT lot, qty_on_hand, cum_before, CASE WHEN cum_before >= 500 THEN 0 WHEN cum_before + qty_on_hand <= 500 THEN qty_on_hand ELSE 500 - cum_before END AS pick_qty FROM (SELECT lot, qty_on_hand, SUM(qty_on_hand) OVER (ORDER BY expiry_date) - qty_on_hand AS cum_before FROM lots) ORDER BY cum_before

messages.content: The pick for 500 jars of jam splits across all three lots, and the split is computed, not eyeballed: lot J-01 contributes 200 of its 200; lot J-02 contributes 200 of its 200; lot J-03 contributes 100 of its 150. The arithmetic per lot is: take nothing if earlier lots already cover the order (cum_before >= 500), take the whole lot if it fits inside the remaining need, else take exactly the remainder - 500 minus what earlier lots supplied. The third lot is the remainder lot: it gives 100 and keeps 50. Printing this as the pick list matters for two reasons. The picker is told quantities per lot, so the lots are emptied in expiry order physically, not just in the system's imagination; and the issue lines posted from the pick carry the lot per quantity, so the stock per lot stays true and any later recall trace knows the order drew 200/200/100 across the three lots. A pick list that just says '500 jars' invites the picker to take all 500 from the nearest pallet - which is always the newest - and quietly converts the two older lots into next month's write-off.

item | on_hand | reserved | available
Hose reel cart | 8 | 8 | 0
Garden hose 30m | 50 | 47 | 3

Availability is a subtraction, and the subtrahend is where the truth lives. The hose shows 50 on hand, but active reservations already claim 47 of them - available is 3. A new order for 5 hoses cannot be promised: 3 - 5 = -2, two short, and promising it anyway is how a shop sells the same hose twice and apologizes once. The LEFT JOIN with COALESCE keeps items with no reservations in the report at full availability instead of dropping them. And available is computed at query time from the two sources, never stored - a stored available figure is a third number that can disagree with both of its parents. A partial receipt of 120 phone chargers just landed against three backorders of 100, 60 and 40 from different dates. Allocate it oldest-first and show me who gets what and who keeps waiting.
I'll queue the backorders by date with a cumulative column and cap each allocation at what the receipt has left:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE backorders (order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, order_date TEXT NOT NULL, qty_wanted INTEGER NOT NULL)

SELECT order_id, order_date, qty_wanted, cum_before, CASE WHEN cum_before >= 120 THEN 0 WHEN cum_before + qty_wanted <= 120 THEN qty_wanted ELSE 120 - cum_before END AS allocated, qty_wanted - (CASE WHEN cum_before >= 120 THEN 0 WHEN cum_before + qty_wanted <= 120 THEN qty_wanted ELSE 120 - cum_before END) AS still_waiting FROM (SELECT order_id, order_date, qty_wanted, SUM(qty_wanted) OVER (ORDER BY order_date, order_id) - qty_wanted AS cum_before FROM backorders) ORDER BY order_date

messages.content: A receipt of 120 chargers lands against 200 units of backorders, and the allocation is oldest-first, computed by the same cumulative pattern as a FEFO pick: order 310 (2026-07-02) wanted 100, gets 100, still waiting 0; order 311 (2026-07-05) wanted 60, gets 20, still waiting 40; order 312 (2026-07-09) wanted 40, gets 0, still waiting 40. Order 310 is made whole, order 311 gets a third of its need and a partial shipment decision (ship 20 now or hold for completeness - a policy question the data cannot answer), and order 312 gets nothing but keeps its place at the head of the queue for the next receipt. Oldest-first is a policy, not a law of nature: allocating by customer value, by promised date, or pro-rata across all three orders are all defensible, and each produces a different table from the same receipt. What is not defensible is allocation by whoever shouts loudest, because it is unrecordable - the cumulative computation's real virtue is that the rule is written in the query, applied identically to everyone, and auditable afterwards when the third customer asks why they waited. Whatever rule you choose, write it down where the query lives, because the queue's fairness is a property of the rule being visible, not of the rule being oldest-first.

1 | 2026-01-12 | 100 | 500 | 0 | 100
2 | 2026-02-09 | 100 | 560 | 100 | 30

FIFO costs an issue by peeling the oldest layers first. The sale of 130 units of olive oil consumes all 100 units of lot 1 at 500 cents, then 30 units of lot 2 at 560 cents: COGS = 100 x 500 + 30 x 560 = 66800 cents. What remains is 70 units of the February layer, so ending inventory is 39200 cents - and the two figures tie: 66800 + 39200 = 106000, the total cost of everything received (100 x 500 + 100 x 560). That tie-out is the FIFO health check: COGS plus ending value must always equal goods available, and when it doesn't, the layer arithmetic - not the market - has a bug. The cumulative-before column is the whole mechanism: each layer knows how many units were consumed before it, so its own consumption is capped at what the issue still needs. Notice the assumption baked in: the units are fungible and the cost flow need not match the physical flow - you may well ship the February oil first; FIFO is a costing convention, and its virtue in a rising market is that ending inventory carries recent, realistic costs while COGS carries the old cheap ones, flattering margin. Know that it flatters, and by how much - that is what the LIFO comparison is for.
Now cost the exact same sale - 130 units, layers of 100 at 500 and 100 at 560 - under LIFO, and tell me precisely how it differs from FIFO and why.
I'll rebuild the same layers and peel them newest-first:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE layers (lot INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, receipt_date TEXT NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL, unit_cost_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)

SELECT lot, receipt_date, qty, unit_cost_cents, CASE WHEN cum_new >= 130 THEN 0 WHEN cum_new + qty <= 130 THEN qty ELSE 130 - cum_new END AS consumed FROM (SELECT lot, receipt_date, qty, unit_cost_cents, SUM(qty) OVER (ORDER BY receipt_date DESC, lot DESC) - qty AS cum_new FROM layers) ORDER BY receipt_date DESC

SELECT SUM(take_qty * unit_cost_cents) FROM (SELECT unit_cost_cents, CASE WHEN cum_new >= 130 THEN 0 WHEN cum_new + qty <= 130 THEN qty ELSE 130 - cum_new END AS take_qty FROM (SELECT qty, unit_cost_cents, SUM(qty) OVER (ORDER BY receipt_date DESC, lot DESC) - qty AS cum_new FROM layers))

messages.content: Same shelves, same sale, opposite convention. LIFO peels the newest layer first: all 100 units of the February lot at 560 cents, then 30 units of January's at 500 - COGS = 100 x 560 + 30 x 500 = 71000 cents, which is 4200 cents more than FIFO's 66800 on the identical transaction. Ending inventory flips the difference: LIFO leaves 70 January units at 500 = 35000 cents, against FIFO's 39200 - the same 4200, sitting in the other statement. Nothing physical differs; the 4200 is purely a decision about which costs are 'the ones we sold'. In a rising market LIFO charges current costs against current revenue (a more honest margin, and in the US a lower tax bill, which is its real constituency) while its balance sheet carries fossil costs - leave LIFO running for a decade and inventory value becomes archaeology. FIFO does the reverse. Neither is the truth; both are conventions with opposite flatteries, which is why IFRS bans LIFO and US GAAP permits it, and why comparing two companies' margins without checking their cost-flow assumption is comparing two different sports. The layer machinery, note, is identical - only the ORDER BY flips from oldest to newest.
We use weighted average cost for screws. Receipts: 100 at 500 cents, then after an issue of 40, another 100 at 560, then an issue of 50. Walk the average through each event and cost both issues.
I'll build the receipts and recompute the pool average at each step:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE receipts (receipt_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, receipt_date TEXT NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL, unit_cost_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT SUM(qty), SUM(qty * unit_cost_cents) FROM receipts WHERE receipt_id = 1

messages.content: Weighted average reprices the whole pool at every receipt, and issues leave at whatever the current average is. Receipt 1: 100 units at 500 - the average is 500. Issue 40 on March 9 leaves at that 500: 20000 cents of COGS, and the pool stands at 60 units worth 30000. Receipt 2 lands March 16: 100 more at 560. The pool is now 160 units worth 30000 + 56000 = 86000, and the average recomputes to 86000 / 160 = 537.5 cents - every unit in the pool, including the cheap January ones, is now carried at 537.5. The March 23 issue of 50 costs 50 x 537.5 = 26875, and the ending position is 110 units at 537.5 = 59125 cents. Check the tie: COGS 20000 + 26875 = 46875, plus ending 59125, equals 106000 - goods available, as it must. The method's character is smoothing: no layer identity survives, price rises leak into COGS gradually instead of all at once, and the per-unit cost of an issue depends on when it happens relative to receipts - the same 50 units cost 25000 before March 16 and 26875 after. That timing sensitivity is the honest price of never having to track layers, and for high-volume fungible stock it is usually worth it. Keep the average at full precision in the data (537.5, not 538): rounding the unit cost at every step quietly creates or destroys cents that the tie-out will later hunt for.

In a falling market both compliments reverse. We sold 60 units in February and another 60 in July, with layers of 100 at 500 (January) and 100 at 620 (June). Why is July's unit cost higher than February's if it's the same product?
I'll cost the first sale, then cost cumulative sales to 120 and take the difference as July's own COGS:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE layers (lot INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, receipt_date TEXT NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL, unit_cost_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)

SELECT SUM(take_qty * unit_cost_cents) FROM (SELECT unit_cost_cents, CASE WHEN cum_before >= 60 THEN 0 WHEN cum_before + qty <= 60 THEN qty ELSE 60 - cum_before END AS take_qty FROM (SELECT qty, unit_cost_cents, SUM(qty) OVER (ORDER BY receipt_date, lot) - qty AS cum_before FROM layers))

SELECT lot, unit_cost_cents, CASE WHEN cum_before >= 120 THEN 0 WHEN cum_before + qty <= 120 THEN qty ELSE 120 - cum_before END AS consumed FROM (SELECT lot, receipt_date, qty, unit_cost_cents, SUM(qty) OVER (ORDER BY receipt_date, lot) - qty AS cum_before FROM layers) ORDER BY receipt_date

SELECT SUM(take_qty * unit_cost_cents) FROM (SELECT unit_cost_cents, CASE WHEN cum_before >= 120 THEN 0 WHEN cum_before + qty <= 120 THEN qty ELSE 120 - cum_before END AS take_qty FROM (SELECT qty, unit_cost_cents, SUM(qty) OVER (ORDER BY receipt_date, lot) - qty AS cum_before FROM layers))

messages.content: The February sale of 60 units costs clean: 60 from the January layer at 500 = 30000 cents, 500 a unit. By July the picture has a seam in it. Cumulative sales reach 120, so the July 60 are costed by continuing the peel: 100 remaining January units at 500, then 20 June units at 620 - the July COGS is 32400 cents, or 540 cents a unit. Identical product, identical quantity, and the July units carry 8% more cost than February's - not because July's selling was worse, but because the January layer ran out mid-sale. This is the number that confuses margin reviews: a gross-margin dip in July that is really a layer boundary crossing. The defense is to read COGS per unit against the layer report before reading it against the sales team: when the per-unit cost steps up exactly when a cheap layer exhausts, the margin story is a purchasing story (the June receipt at 620 is the event), and the selling story may be blameless. Costs in a FIFO system have a memory, and the memory's length is however long your layers last.
Our FIFO costing for one item looks too low this month. Receipts were 90 at 300 and 60 at 340, but sales show 180 units. Can you run the costing and tell me if the number can be trusted?
I'll total receipts and sales first, then run the layer costing and compare what it actually covered:

CREATE TABLE sales (sale_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, qty INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO sales VALUES (1, 70), (2, 60), (3, 50)

SELECT SUM(qty) FROM sales

SELECT SUM(take_qty * unit_cost_cents) FROM (SELECT unit_cost_cents, CASE WHEN cum_before >= 180 THEN 0 WHEN cum_before + qty <= 180 THEN qty ELSE 180 - cum_before END AS take_qty FROM (SELECT qty, unit_cost_cents, SUM(qty) OVER (ORDER BY receipt_date, lot) - qty AS cum_before FROM layers))

messages.content: Something is wrong before any costing starts: receipts total 150 units but sales total 180 - 30 units were sold that were never received, at least not in this table. Watch what the FIFO query does with that: it dutifully costs the first 150 units from the layers (47400 cents) and costs the remaining 30 at nothing at all, because there is no layer left to take them from. The CASE caps each layer's consumption, the uncovered units fall through every branch, and the COGS comes out understated by 30 units' worth - silently, with a plausible-looking total. That silence is the lesson. A FIFO (or LIFO, or average) computation cannot detect that its inputs are impossible; it will cost a negative inventory position at zero and move on. The integrity check belongs upstream of the costing: units sold must never exceed units received plus opening stock, per item, and the exception list from that check is a data-quality report - here it says a receipt is missing, a sale was double-posted, or an opening balance was never loaded, and until one of those is found, every margin computed for this item is fiction with good formatting. Never let a costing query be the first place an impossible quantity surfaces.

Lot W-11: 40 bags at 8000 cents cost, recoverable as seconds at 3000 - a write-down of 200000 cents, carrying value 120000. Lot W-14's totes take a smaller one (22500 cents). The healthy lots (recoverable NULL or equal to cost) write down nothing. In total: cost 477500 cents becomes carrying value 700000 cents, a write-down of 222500 cents recognized now, in the period the damage was discovered - not dripped into future COGS as the bags slowly sell at a loss. Three disciplines keep NRV honest. The recoverable figure must be evidence (a seconds-channel price, a salvage quote), not optimism - an inflated recoverable is just an unbooked loss. The write-down is one-way in most frameworks: if the bags later sell for more, the gain appears at sale, not by writing the lot back up. And the adjustment is posted as its own valuation movement against the lot, with the damage report referenced, so the lot's history reads 'cost 8000, written to 3000 on the flood report' rather than the cost quietly becoming 3000 in an edit that erases the event.

INSERT INTO receipts VALUES (1, 'FreshFarms', 500, 500), (2, 'FreshFarms', 400, 398), (3, 'FreshFarms', 600, 600), (4, 'ValleyPack', 300, 294), (5, 'ValleyPack', 250, 245), (6, 'ValleyPack', 350, 343), (7, 'OrchardCo', 200, 200), (8, 'OrchardCo', 180, 179)

messages.content:
supplier | deliveries | ordered | received | short_units | short_pct
ValleyPack | 3 | 900 | 882 | 18 | 2
OrchardCo | 2 | 380 | 379 | 1 | 0.2631578947
FreshFarms | 3 | 1500 | 1498 | 2 | 0.1333333333

The dock tells a consistent story: ValleyPack: 18 units short on 900 ordered (2%) across 3 deliveries; OrchardCo: 1 units short on 380 ordered (0.2631578947%) across 2 deliveries; FreshFarms: 2 units short on 1500 ordered (0.1333333333%) across 3 deliveries. Can you compute the damage rate by storage bin? Raw counts mislead because the bins handle different volumes - I want damage as a share of throughput.
I'll aggregate write-offs against total throughput per bin and rank the rates:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE movements (movement_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, location TEXT NOT NULL, qty_change INTEGER NOT NULL, movement_type TEXT NOT NULL, reason_code TEXT)

INSERT INTO movements VALUES (1, 'Bin A', 800, 'receipt', NULL), (2, 'Bin A', -610, 'issue', NULL), (3, 'Bin A', -9, 'write_off', 'damaged'), (4, 'Bin B', 800, 'receipt', NULL), (5, 'Bin B', -590, 'issue', NULL), (6, 'Bin B', -34, 'write_off', 'damaged'), (7, 'Bin C', 800, 'receipt', NULL), (8, 'Bin C', -640, 'issue', NULL), (9, 'Bin C', -7, 'write_off', 'damaged'), (10, 'Bin D', 800, 'receipt', NULL), (11, 'Bin D', -605, 'issue', NULL), (12, 'Bin D', -11, 'write_off', 'damaged')

SELECT location, -SUM(CASE WHEN movement_type = 'write_off' THEN qty_change END) AS damaged, SUM(CASE WHEN movement_type != 'write_off' THEN ABS(qty_change) END) AS throughput, (-SUM(CASE WHEN movement_type = 'write_off' THEN qty_change END)) * 100.0 / SUM(CASE WHEN movement_type != 'write_off' THEN ABS(qty_change) END) AS damage_pct FROM movements GROUP BY location ORDER BY damage_pct DESC

messages.content: Damage normalized by throughput - because a busy bin should break more in absolute terms: Bin B: 34 damaged on 1390 units of throughput (2.4460431655%); Bin D: 11 damaged on 1405 units of throughput (0.7829181495%); Bin A: 9 damaged on 1410 units of throughput (0.6382978723%); Bin C: 7 damaged on 1440 units of throughput (0.4861111111%). Bin B is the outlier at 2.4460431655% - about five times the rate of the gentlest bin on the same goods and the same 800 units received. Throughput normalization is what makes the comparison honest: raw counts would rank Bin B worst too, but only the rate proves it isn't just the busiest bin. A location-shaped damage rate has location-shaped causes: Bin B is under the leaking pipe, at the end of the forklift turn, stacked one layer too high, or worked by a crew that was never shown the handling rule - the query cannot choose, but it has reduced a warehouse-wide question to a single bin's inspection list. This is the general move for damage: never report a global damage count, because a global count has no address. Damage by location, by shift, by supplier, by week - the rate is only useful when it is attached to something a person can go and look at.
Do expired write-offs count as shrinkage? Our seasonal stock gap mixes both and I want to see how much the answer changes the shrinkage figure.
I'll compute the total gap, then show the residual under both classification treatments:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE items (item TEXT PRIMARY KEY, book_qty INTEGER NOT NULL, counted_qty INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO items VALUES ('Seasonal candles', 300, 282), ('Gift wrap rolls', 500, 471), ('Calendars 2026', 220, 196)
CREATE TABLE movements (movement_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, item TEXT NOT NULL, qty_change INTEGER NOT NULL, movement_type TEXT NOT NULL, reason_code TEXT)
INSERT INTO movements VALUES (1, 'Calendars 2026', -24, 'write_off', 'expired'), (2, 'Seasonal candles', -6, 'write_off', 'damaged'), (3, 'Gift wrap rolls', -4, 'write_off', 'damaged')
SELECT SUM(book_qty) - SUM(counted_qty) FROM items
SELECT -SUM(qty_change) FROM movements WHERE movement_type = 'write_off'

messages.content: The gap between book and counted across these seasonal lines is 71 units, and 34 of them are already explained by logged write-offs - leaving a shrinkage residual of 37 units, 52.1126760563% of the gap. But watch what the classification choice does. The 24 calendars were written off as 'expired' - they became worthless on January 1 by the calendar, not by anyone's carelessness. If your policy counts expiry write-offs as shrinkage, the residual above stands. If expiry is reported in its own obsolescence line (the treatment I would defend - expiry is a buying failure, not a custody failure), the write-off explanation drops to 10 and the unexplained residual rises to 61 units, 85.9154929577% of the gap. The lesson is that 'shrinkage rate' is a policy decision before it is a measurement: what counts as shrinkage (theft only? all unexplained? unexplained plus expiry?) must be written down, or the number will drift with whoever compiles it and quarter-on-quarter comparisons become meaningless. Pick the definition that separates custody problems from buying problems, state it on the report, and never change it silently - a redefinition is a restatement.
Can you trend our monthly shrinkage over the last six months? Raw missing units keep rising but so is the store, so give me the rate.
I'll compute each month's count gap as a percentage of that month's book stock:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE count_adjustments (adj_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, month TEXT NOT NULL, book_qty INTEGER NOT NULL, counted_qty INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT month, book_qty - counted_qty AS missing, (book_qty - counted_qty) * 100.0 / book_qty AS shrink_pct FROM count_adjustments ORDER BY month

messages.content: Six months of count adjustments, as a rate rather than raw units - because the store grew over the same period, and raw missing units would confuse growth with leakage: 2026-04: 53 missing (1.0192307692%); 2026-05: 61 missing (1.1401869159%); 2026-06: 84 missing (1.5328467153%); 2026-07: 112 missing (2%); 2026-08: 99 missing (1.7307692308%); 2026-09: 80 missing (1.3675213675%). The story is the July peak: the rate climbs from June's 1.5328467153% to 2% in July - about double where April started - and then partially recovers in August (1.7307692308%) and September (1.3675213675%). A step change has a date, and a date has a cause - something changed at the start of July: a new shift pattern, a relocated high-value fixture, a receiving process edit, a seasonal temp crew. The trend table's job is to hand the investigation that date. Two reading disciplines: always trend the rate, not the units, in a growing business; and distrust single-month moves - counts are noisy, a miscounted fast line swings a month - which is why the partial recovery matters: it says July was an event, not a new normal, while three consecutive rises would say the opposite. Pair the monthly rate with the cause-coded write-offs and the picture completes: the trend says when, the codes say what, and neither is much use alone.
Our flour supplier quotes 5-day delivery. I have our last 10 PO and receipt dates - what lead time should we actually plan against?
I'll compute the actual lead time of each delivery and look at the distribution, not the brochure:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE receipts (po INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, order_date TEXT NOT NULL, receipt_date TEXT NOT NULL)
SELECT po, CAST(julianday(receipt_date) - julianday(order_date) AS INTEGER) AS lead_days FROM receipts ORDER BY lead_days
SELECT AVG(julianday(receipt_date) - julianday(order_date)), MIN(julianday(receipt_date) - julianday(order_date)), MAX(julianday(receipt_date) - julianday(order_date)) FROM receipts

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
AVG(julianday(receipt_date) - julianday(order_date)) | MIN(julianday(receipt_date) - julianday(order_date)) | MAX(julianday(receipt_date) - julianday(order_date))
6 | 4 | 12

Ten measured lead times for the flour contract, sorted: 4, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 6, 6, 7, 12 days. The average is 6 days - and the average is the number that causes stockouts, because half of reality is worse than it. The 90th percentile - the 9th of the 10 sorted values - is 7 days: nine deliveries in ten arrived within that. Plan against the p90 and you are covered for the normal bad case; the maximum (12 days, the March order) is the disaster case, which safety stock alone should not try to absorb. Put money on the difference: at 9 units a day of usage, planning on the average (6 days) covers 54 units of lead-time demand, while the p90 plan covers 63 - the extra 9 units are the honest price of the supplier's variability, charged to the supplier's inconsistency rather than to your customers' empty shelf. Measure lead time from your own PO and receipt dates, never from the supplier's brochure: the brochure number is a sales document, and the gap between it and the measured p90 is usually where the stockouts live.
Can you score our three produce suppliers on on-time delivery from the promised versus received dates?
I'll build the delivery log and score each supplier on on-time fraction and average slippage:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE deliveries (po INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, supplier TEXT NOT NULL, promised_date TEXT NOT NULL, received_date TEXT NOT NULL)

SELECT supplier, COUNT(*) AS deliveries, SUM(CASE WHEN received_date <= promised_date THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS on_time, SUM(CASE WHEN received_date <= promised_date THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) * 100.0 / COUNT(*) AS on_time_pct, AVG(julianday(received_date) - julianday(promised_date)) AS avg_days_vs_promise FROM deliveries GROUP BY supplier ORDER BY on_time_pct DESC

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
supplier | deliveries | on_time | on_time_pct | avg_days_vs_promise
OrchardCo | 4 | 3 | 75 | 0.25
FreshFarms | 5 | 3 | 60 | 1
ValleyPack | 3 | 0 | 0 | 2

The scorecard, where on time means received on or before the promised date: OrchardCo: 3 of 4 on time (75%), averaging 0.25 days against promise; FreshFarms: 3 of 5 on time (60%), averaging 1 days against promise; ValleyPack: 0 of 3 on time (0%), averaging 2 days against promise. Read the two columns together, because they catch different sins. The fraction says how often a supplier breaks a promise; the average slippage says how much it matters - a supplier late by a day every time is a planning input (pad the promise by one day and they become perfectly predictable), while a supplier on time 90% of the time but nine days late on the miss is a stockout machine wearing a good score. Also interrogate the promise itself: these dates are the supplier's own commitments, so a 100% score against padded promises is less impressive than 85% against tight ones - which is why the scorecard belongs in the contract conversation, where the promise definition gets agreed, not just in the warehouse, where it gets suffered. Scorecards measured from your own receipts are the only version a supplier cannot argue with, because every row is a delivery they made to you.

supplier | units | share_pct | avg_cost
MillDirect | 1200 | 66.6666666667 | 483.75
AgriWholesale | 600 | 33.3333333333 | 514.1666666667

Our toner supplier has a 500-unit minimum order but we only use 12 a day. Can you show how much forced overstock an MOQ creates, for toner and for paper?
I'll set usage, lead time and MOQ side by side and compute the excess each order forces:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE items (item TEXT PRIMARY KEY, daily_usage REAL NOT NULL, lead_days INTEGER NOT NULL, moq INTEGER NOT NULL, unit_cost_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO items VALUES ('Printer toner cartridge', 12, 6, 500, 3900), ('A4 paper case', 30, 4, 100, 2400)

SELECT item, daily_usage, lead_days, moq, daily_usage * lead_days AS lead_need, moq - daily_usage * lead_days AS excess_units, (moq - daily_usage * lead_days) * unit_cost_cents AS excess_value_cents, moq * 1.0 / daily_usage AS days_to_consume FROM items

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
item | daily_usage | lead_days | moq | lead_need | excess_units | excess_value_cents | days_to_consume
Printer toner cartridge | 12 | 6 | 500 | 72 | 428 | 1669200 | 41.6666666667
A4 paper case | 30 | 4 | 100 | 120 | -20 | -48000 | 3.3333333333

The toner line is the MOQ trap in pure arithmetic. Usage is 12 cartridges a day and lead time is 6 days, so a reorder cycle genuinely needs 72 units of cover. The supplier's minimum order is 500. Every order therefore forces 428 excess units onto the shelf - 1669200 cents of stock bought not because demand asked for it but because the contract did - and takes 41.6666666667 days to work through, by which time the printer fleet may have changed models. The paper case shows the same computation with a benign answer: lead-time need is 120 against an MOQ of 100, so the minimum never binds (the computed excess is -20 - the need already exceeds the minimum) and the order takes 3.3333333333 days to consume - MOQs only hurt when the minimum dwarfs the lead-time need. The responses, in order of preference: negotiate the MOQ against a committed annual volume (the supplier's real concern is total throughput, not per-order size); consolidate SKUs so one item's order carries the volume; share the order across locations; or accept the overstock with open eyes and cost it - the excess value column, per order, times orders per year, is the number that belongs in the contract renewal, because 'your MOQ costs us X a year in forced stock' is an argument, and 'your MOQ is annoying' is not.
We stocked out of oat milk in August and I think a late delivery caused it. PO 77 was due August 7. Can you join the delivery to the stock movements and the unfilled orders and show me the chain?
I'll walk the balance day by day, check the PO's lateness, and count what went unfilled:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE purchase_orders (po INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, item TEXT NOT NULL, promised_date TEXT NOT NULL, received_date TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO purchase_orders VALUES (77, 'Oat milk 1L', '2026-08-07', '2026-08-11')
CREATE TABLE movements (movement_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, move_date TEXT NOT NULL, qty_change INTEGER NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE orders (order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, order_date TEXT NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL, filled INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT move_date, SUM(qty_change) OVER (ORDER BY move_date, movement_id) AS balance FROM movements
SELECT SUM(qty), COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE filled = 0
SELECT CAST(julianday(received_date) - julianday(promised_date) AS INTEGER) FROM purchase_orders WHERE po = 77

messages.content: PO 77 was promised August 7 and arrived August 11 - 4 days late. The balance walk shows why those 4 days matter: receipts and issues brought the oat milk to exactly zero on 2026-08-08, and the shelf stayed empty until the late delivery landed on the 11th. In that window, 2 orders totalling 20 units went unfilled - real demand, recorded as orders the system could not serve. Note the near-miss inside the story - on the promised date itself the balance stood at just 5 units, one day of issues from empty, so the shelf had almost nothing left to absorb the delay; the reorder that feeds this item runs with very little slack. Two suppliers average almost the same lead time but one feels much riskier. Can you quantify the variability difference?
I'll measure each supplier's lead-time range and spread, not just the average:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE receipts (po INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, supplier TEXT NOT NULL, order_date TEXT NOT NULL, receipt_date TEXT NOT NULL)

SELECT supplier, COUNT(*) AS deliveries, MIN(julianday(receipt_date) - julianday(order_date)) AS min_lead, AVG(julianday(receipt_date) - julianday(order_date)) AS avg_lead, MAX(julianday(receipt_date) - julianday(order_date)) AS max_lead, MAX(julianday(receipt_date) - julianday(order_date)) - MIN(julianday(receipt_date) - julianday(order_date)) AS spread FROM receipts GROUP BY supplier ORDER BY spread DESC

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
supplier | deliveries | min_lead | avg_lead | max_lead | spread
SwingCo | 4 | 1 | 4.5 | 8 | 7
SteadyCo | 4 | 4 | 4.5 | 5 | 1

Two suppliers, nearly the same average, entirely different risks. SwingCo: 4 deliveries, lead times from 1 to 8 days, average 4.5, a spread of 7 days. SteadyCo: 4 deliveries, 4 to 5 days, average 4.5, spread of 1. If you planned both on their averages you would hold the same cover for both - and SwingCo would stock you out regularly while SteadyCo never did. Variability, not slowness, is what safety stock exists to absorb: the steady supplier at 5 days needs almost no buffer because the 5 is trustworthy, while the swing supplier's buffer must cover the gap between their average and their bad tail. This is why lead-time variability belongs on the scorecard next to the average and the on-time rate: the three numbers describe different failure modes (slow, unreliable against promise, unpredictable), they have different fixes (negotiate, enforce, buffer), and they price differently. A supplier who is slow but metronomic is often the better partner - you can plan around a constant; you can only pad against a variance, and padding is inventory, and inventory is money sitting still.

OrchardCo | 600 | 591 | 98.5

SELECT AVG(freight_cents) FROM receipts WHERE rush = 0

That premium is a symptom with a price tag. Each rush order is a small confession that planning missed - a reorder point set too low, a lead time trusted from a brochure, a demand spike nobody flagged - and the freight premium is the mildest cost of the miss, next to the stockout risk that made someone pick up the phone. Trending the premium quarter over quarter turns 'we expedite a lot' into a number a planning fix can be measured against: fix the reorder points and watch this line fall. One data discipline makes the whole report possible: rush must be a flag on the receipt at receiving time, with the freight actually charged - reconstructed later from memory it will always be understated, because nobody remembers the routine saves, only the heroic ones. And the baseline matters: premium-over-standard, not total rush freight, is the honest figure, since the goods had to travel somehow in every timeline.

Definitions do the heavy lifting in this metric, so state them: end-of-day balance is the conservative choice (a day that sold its last unit at noon still counts as stocked, which flatters the figure slightly; an intraday measure would be harsher and usually isn't available). What availability must never be is a snapshot of today generalized, or an average balance dressed up as a percentage. 86.6667% also needs its translation: it means a customer arriving on a random October day had roughly a one-in-seven chance of finding the shelf empty - for a staple that anchors a basket, that is a loyalty number, not a logistics footnote. Report availability per item over a stated window with the zero days listed; the list is what turns the percentage from a grade into a work queue.
Our dashboard showed average coffee bean stock of about 210 for October and called it healthy, but customers hit empty shelves twice. Can you show me what the average hid?
I'll put the average next to the minimum and the zero-day count from the same snapshots:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE snapshots (day TEXT PRIMARY KEY, end_balance INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT AVG(end_balance), MIN(end_balance), MAX(end_balance), SUM(CASE WHEN end_balance = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) FROM snapshots
