messages.content:
AVG(end_balance) | MIN(end_balance) | MAX(end_balance) | SUM(CASE WHEN end_balance = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
209.0333333333 | 0 | 258 | 2

The dashboard said the coffee beans averaged 209.0333333333 units in October - a plump, healthy number. The same table's minimum is 0, and the zero count is 2: the shelf stood empty on two separate days, the 12th and the 23rd, in a month whose average never looked troubled. This is the average's structural lie for inventory: stock is not a level to be averaged, it is a floor that must never be crossed, and an average over a period that includes both the delivery-day peaks (240) and the zero days reports the one thing customers never experience. Nobody buys the average; they buy on a day, and on two days the answer was nothing. The honest dashboard trio for any item is minimum balance, zero-day count, and availability percentage - the average can stay for capacity planning, where it belongs, but it should never again be the headline for service. When a metric can look healthiest precisely when deliveries are large and infrequent (big peaks dragging the average up while the gaps between them empty the shelf), the metric is not merely uninformative, it is reassuring in exactly the dangerous direction.
Price the coconut water stockout for me: the shelf hit zero on October 14 and the next receipt was October 18. What demand went unfilled in the window, in units and cents?
I'll bound the zero window from the movements and sum the unfilled orders inside it:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE movements (movement_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, move_date TEXT NOT NULL, qty_change INTEGER NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE orders (order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, order_date TEXT NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL, unit_price_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, filled INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT move_date, SUM(qty_change) OVER (ORDER BY move_date, movement_id) AS balance FROM movements
SELECT SUM(qty), SUM(qty * unit_price_cents), COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE filled = 0

messages.content: The coconut water's zero window runs from October 14 (the day the balance reached zero) until the receipt on the 18th. The orders that fell into it: 3 orders, 56 units, 19600 cents of demand the shelf could not serve. The first order after the receipt, on the 18th, filled normally - the loss is bounded by the window, which is what makes it countable. Two honesty notes on that 19600. First, unfilled is not identical to lost: some of those customers may have waited, substituted, or returned - the orders table records demand refused, and treating it all as lost revenue is the conservative-for-learning, aggressive-for-reporting choice; say which you are doing. Second, the figure excludes the invisible loss - the customers who saw the empty shelf and never placed an order at all. Recorded unfilled demand is the floor of the true cost, never the ceiling. Even as a floor it does its job: it converts a stockout from an anecdote ('we were out for a few days') into a priced event that can be compared against the cost of the buffer stock that would have prevented it. That comparison - lost margin per stockout against holding cost per unit of safety stock - is the entire economics of service levels, and it can only be run when unfilled orders are recorded rather than evaporating at the shelf edge.

CREATE TABLE movements (movement_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, move_date TEXT NOT NULL, qty_change INTEGER NOT NULL)

SELECT CAST(julianday(order_date) - julianday('2026-04-02') AS INTEGER), CAST(julianday(receipt_date) - julianday('2026-04-11') AS INTEGER) FROM purchase_orders WHERE po = 31

6 | 3

The rice timeline has two failures in it, and the ledger separates them cleanly. The balance crossed the reorder point of 120 on 2026-04-02 (118 after that day's issue). The purchase order was not placed until April 8 - 6 days later, six days in which the stock fell from 118 to 35 with no order in flight. The shelf hit zero on 2026-04-11, and the receipt arrived April 14, 3 days after that. Total time from signal to stockout: nine days. Time from signal to order: 6 of them. The supplier's six-day delivery (April 8 to 14) was not even the problem - had the order been placed on the crossing day, the same six-day delivery lands on April 8 with 35 units still on the shelf, and there is no stockout at all. This is why the crossing-to-order gap belongs in every stockout postmortem: reorder points are usually blamed ('set it higher') when the actual failure is latency - a report run weekly, a buyer on leave, an approval queue. Raising the ROP to cover a six-day human delay works, but it taxes every cycle forever for a process failure that an alert on the crossing day would fix for free. Measure the gap before you touch the policy.
The eggs stocked out briefly in April. PO was promised April 10. Can you reconstruct exactly how long we were out and why?
I'll date the zero point and the delivery's lateness from the two tables:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE purchase_orders (po INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, item TEXT NOT NULL, promised_date TEXT NOT NULL, received_date TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO purchase_orders VALUES (9, 'Free-range eggs 12pk', '2026-04-10', '2026-04-12')
CREATE TABLE movements (movement_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, move_date TEXT NOT NULL, qty_change INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT move_date, SUM(qty_change) OVER (ORDER BY move_date, movement_id) AS balance FROM movements
SELECT CAST(julianday(received_date) - julianday(promised_date) AS INTEGER) FROM purchase_orders WHERE po = 9

messages.content: A small, clean timeline. The eggs sold down through the 9th and the balance reached zero at close on 2026-04-10 - the promised delivery date itself. The delivery actually arrived on the 12th, 2 days late, and was booked at close, so the shelf stood empty for exactly two trading days: the 11th and the 12th. Selling resumed on the 13th. Two days of lateness, two days of stockout - the one-to-one mapping is the point. There was no buffer to absorb any of the delay: the stock was planned to reach zero on the day the delivery was due, which means the plan treated the promise as a certainty. A plan that lands at zero on the promise date has quietly decided that the supplier's promise is a physical law. The proportionate fix is not a mountain of eggs - eggs expire - it is a one-to-two-day cover on this line (roughly one average day's issue, about 30 units here) or a promise date negotiated with the lateness distribution in mind. Short, bounded stockouts like this one are the cheapest tuition in inventory management: the timeline is fully reconstructable, the cause is singular, and the fix is small. Log it, price the two days, adjust the cover, move on.

The dairy category's true exposure is concentrated in one promise date. The mitigations are structural: stagger the two lines' order cycles so their promise dates differ, qualify a backup for one of the lines (splitting the pair across suppliers breaks the correlation), or hold the buffer on the pair jointly sized for a shared delay. What does not work is investigating the butter and the cream as two separate incidents with two separate owners - the incident was the truck.
Can you analyze the sourdough's stockouts over the last 60 days as spells - how many separate outages, how long each, and the overall availability?
I'll find the zero days and group consecutive ones into spells with the island technique:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE snapshots (day TEXT PRIMARY KEY, end_balance INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(CASE WHEN end_balance = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) FROM snapshots

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
COUNT(*) | SUM(CASE WHEN end_balance = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
60 | 7

arguments.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM snapshots z WHERE z.end_balance = 0 AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM snapshots p WHERE p.day = date(z.day, '-1 day') AND p.end_balance = 0)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS spell_len FROM (SELECT day, julianday(day) - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY day) AS island FROM snapshots WHERE end_balance = 0) GROUP BY island ORDER BY spell_len DESC

messages.content: Sixty days of sourdough snapshots resolve into 3 distinct stockout spells totalling 7 zero days - spell lengths 4, 2, 1 - for an availability of 88.3333333333%. The spell structure says more than the total. A single 7-day spell would point at one supply failure; three spells of 2, 1 and 4 days point at a rhythm - the bakery's delivery cycle keeps nearly missing, and the misses cluster as short gaps with one longer one in mid-October. Frequency and duration are different problems: frequent short spells are a timing/order-cycle issue, rare long spells are a supplier-reliability issue, and the remedies (order a day earlier versus qualify a second bakery) do not substitute for each other. The island trick in the query - grouping zero days by date minus row number, so consecutive days share a group - is worth keeping in your pocket: spell analysis is the difference between 'availability 88%' as a grade and 'three spells, longest four days, worsening' as a diagnosis. Always report spells alongside the percentage; the percentage alone cannot tell a bad week from a bad system.
Our availability report shows the decorative candles at 100% for the whole quarter - best in the store. Something about that feels wrong. Can you check it against demand?
I'll set the availability figure next to the quarter's actual issues for the same item:

arguments.sql: SELECT COALESCE(-SUM(qty_change), 0) FROM movements WHERE movement_type = 'issue'

messages.content: The decorative candles post a perfect quarter: 92 of 92 days in stock, availability 100%, never fewer than 138 units on the shelf. And total issues for the quarter: 0. Nothing sold. Not one unit. Availability measures the presence of stock, not the presence of demand - a shelf can be perfectly available and perfectly pointless, and this metric will award it full marks every quarter while the capital sits in wax. The candles are not a service success; they are dead stock with a flawless availability score, and the two reports side by side are the whole lesson: availability must always be read next to issues (or turns, or days-since-last-issue), because each metric alone has a blind spot the other covers. Availability without demand hides dead stock; demand without availability hides lost sales. There is a subtler corruption too: teams measured on availability learn to keep unloved stock forever (delisting hurts the metric) and to fear lean positions on fast lines (a stockout hurts more than a warehouse of candles helps). Pair the metrics in the same report, always, and let the pair argue - the argument is the insight.

messages.content: The whole milk stockout, end to end, every interval measured. November 3: the balance closes at 85, crossing the reorder point of 90 - the signal fires. November 6: the PO is placed, 3 days after the signal - response latency. November 8: the balance reaches zero, the day before the promise date, because issues ran hot (32 on the 8th alone). November 9: the promised date passes with no delivery. November 11: the receipt lands, 2 days late against promise and 3 days after the shelf emptied. Unfilled demand across the window: 41 units. Three causes, three owners, one event. The 3-day ordering latency is a process fix (alert on crossing, don't batch POs twice a week). The demand heat is a forecasting note (early-November issues ran above the rate the ROP was set from). The 2-day supplier lateness is a scorecard entry. Any single-cause story - 'the supplier was late' - would have fixed a third of the problem and guaranteed a rerun. This is the complete postmortem shape, and it generalizes: signal date, response date, zero date, promise date, recovery date, unfilled quantity, each computed from the ledger rather than remembered. Run it for every stockout of an A item, file the five dates, and within a quarter the pattern across events - which interval is systematically the fat one - tells you where the system, not the week, is broken.
